lessons.title: Common Valuation Traps: Peak Margins, Value Traps and Multiple Mean Reversion

children.text: You now have the full toolkit: cash flows, discount rates, terminal value, multiples, peer sets and methods matched to business types. What remains is knowing how those tools fail in practice. Most money lost on valuation is not lost through arithmetic errors. It is lost through a handful of repeatable judgement errors, and the same ones appear again and again in Indian markets.

body.text: Almost every valuation mistake is the same mistake in disguise: treating something temporary as permanent, or something permanent as temporary. Peak margins, current multiples and this year's growth rate are temporary. Weak returns on capital, poor governance and structural decline are usually permanent.

children.text: The Traps, in One Table

cells: Peak margins
A cyclical or commodity-linked company at record profitability, extrapolated for a decade
Normalise margins over a full cycle
Value trap
A cheap multiple on a business in structural decline or with poor governance
Check ROCE against WACC, and ask why it is cheap
Multiple mean reversion
Assuming a high multiple stays, or a low one returns to its historical median
Decompose expected return into growth, yield and multiple change
Reinvesting at low returns
Growth funded by capital earning less than it costs
Compare return on new capital with WACC
Ignoring dilution
Per-share value forgotten while total value grows
Model equity raises and ESOPs explicitly
Precision illusion
A value quoted to two decimals from a model with a dozen guesses
Present ranges and scenarios
Anchoring
Adjusting the discount rate until the DCF agrees with the market price or your view
Set the discount rate before you see the answer
Double counting
Growth in the cash flows and again in the exit multiple; cash added twice
Check the bridge and reconcile methods

children.text: Trap 1: Peak Margins

A company earns ₹10,000 crore of revenue. In a strong year its EBIT margin reaches 18.0%; across a full cycle it averages 11.0%. Value it as a perpetuity at a 11.0% cost of capital, 5.0% growth and a 15.0% return on new capital, and the difference is not subtle.

body.title: Same company, two margin assumptions (₹ crore of enterprise value)

body.label: The cost of extrapolating a peak
body.context: Valuing on a normalised 11.0% margin instead of the peak 18.0% cuts enterprise value from ₹15,750 crore to ₹9,625 crore. Nothing about the business changed, only which year you believed.

children.text: Peak margins are easiest to spot in metals, cement and sugar, but they appear everywhere: a chemicals company benefiting from a competitor's plant shutdown, an exporter helped by a weak rupee, a lender with unusually low credit costs, an FMCG company enjoying a collapse in palm oil prices. The test is always the same: compare this year's margin with the seven to ten year average, and ask what specifically caused the difference.
Trap 2: The Value Trap
A
value trap
is the mirror image of a peak-margin mistake: instead of paying for profits that will not last, you buy a discount that never closes. The multiple is low for a reason you have not identified.

markDefs.definition: A stock that looks cheap on conventional multiples but whose business is deteriorating, so the low multiple is justified and the price keeps falling or stagnating.

columns.label: Signs of a genuine bargain
points: ROCE consistently above the cost of capital, including in weak years
The problem is cyclical or temporary, and you can name it
Cash flows still cover dividends and capex
Management has a record of sensible capital allocation
A specific catalyst exists: capacity coming on stream, a demerger, a turnaround plan with milestones

columns.label: Signs of a value trap
points: ROCE below the cost of capital for years
Structural decline: the product or channel is being replaced
Repeated equity raises, related-party transactions, promoter pledging
The only argument for buying is the low multiple itself

children.text: Why reinvestment makes a value trap worse
Take a company earning 9.0% on equity against a 12.0% cost of equity, and reinvesting 60.0% of its profits to grow at 5.4%. Compare that with the same company paying everything out as dividends.

stats.label: Justified P/E if it pays everything out
Value destroyed by growing
stats.context: Each retained rupee is worth less than a rupee

body.text: This is the cruellest feature of a value trap. A company earning less than its cost of capital becomes less valuable the faster it grows, because every rupee retained is worth less than the rupee returned to you. A cheap multiple plus an ambitious expansion plan is a worse combination than a cheap multiple alone.

children.text: Trap 3: Assuming Multiples Mean Revert

Investors on both sides make this mistake. One buys a high-multiple compounder assuming the multiple holds forever. Another buys a derated stock assuming the multiple returns to its ten-year median. Neither is a fact, and the arithmetic of the multiple change often dominates everything else.

body.caption: Over long periods, these three components explain almost all of an equity return

children.text: Take a company growing EPS at 12.0% with a 1.0% dividend yield, bought at 30 times earnings.

body.caption: What happens to your return when the multiple changes

cells: P/E holds at 30×
P/E falls 30× to 25× over 5 years
P/E falls 30× to 20× over 5 years
P/E falls 30× to 20× over 10 years

children.text: If EPS grows 12.0% a year for 5 years, it ends at 1.12⁵ = 1.76 times today's level. If the P/E falls from 30 to 20, the price ends at 1.76 × (20 ÷ 30) = 1.17 times today's price.
Annualised, that is 1.17^(1/5) - 1 = 3.3% a year, plus a 1.0% dividend yield. Strong earnings growth of 12.0% has been reduced to a total return of 4.3% by the derating alone.
The same derating spread over 10 years costs far less per year, because the multiple change is amortised over a longer period: a total return of 8.5%.

body.text: This cuts both ways, and it is why Chapter 4 insisted on checking whether a historical median is still relevant. If you buy a stock at 15 times that deserves 15 times, your return is roughly growth plus yield. If you buy at 30 times a business that will settle at 20 times, you need exceptional growth simply to stand still.

children.text: Trap 4: Forgetting Dilution

A company you value at ₹200 per share issues 25 crore new shares at ₹140, a discount to that value, to fund expansion. The total value of the company rises, because it now holds the cash raised, but your share of it falls.

This is why the Chapter 3 bridge insisted on a fully diluted share count, and why loss-making companies that must keep raising capital deserve extra caution. Total enterprise value is not what you own. Value per share is.
Trap 5: Precision, Anchoring and Double Counting
Precision illusion.
A DCF that outputs ₹1,247.38 invites false confidence. Quote a range, show the sensitivity table, and name the two assumptions that drive the answer.
Anchoring to the market price.

Choosing a discount rate or growth rate that makes the model agree with the current price defeats the purpose. Set the inputs first, then look at the answer, then use a reverse DCF to understand the gap.
Anchoring to your purchase price.
The price you paid is irrelevant to what a business is worth today. So is the 52-week high.
Double counting growth.
Forecasting high growth in the cash flows and then applying a growth-inflated exit multiple counts the same optimism twice.
Double counting cash.
Adding surplus cash to enterprise value while also counting the interest it earns inside the operating forecast.
Ignoring the tax shield rule.
Using an after-tax cost of debt in WACC and also adding back the interest tax saving in the cash flows.
Check Your Understanding

body.title: The cost of a derating
body.prompt: You buy a stock at 28 times earnings. Over the next five years EPS grows 10% a year, but the P/E falls to 18. What is the annualised price return, in %? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: EPS ends at 1.10⁵ = 1.61 times today's. The price ends at 1.61 × (18 ÷ 28) = 1.04 times today's. Annualised: 0.7% a year. Ten percent earnings growth delivered a return close to nothing, because the multiple did the opposite.

body.title: Normalising a peak margin
body.prompt: A commodity chemicals company earns ₹10,000 crore of revenue at a peak EBIT margin of 18%, against a ten-year average of 11%. Using the same perpetuity assumptions for both, by what percentage does enterprise value fall when you use the normalised margin instead of the peak? Answer to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: Value scales directly with the margin here, so the fall is 1 - (11 ÷ 18) = 38.9%. In the worked example, enterprise value drops from ₹15,750 crore to ₹9,625 crore.

body.title: Bargain or trap?
body.question: A listed company trades at 7 times earnings and 0.6 times book. Its ROCE has averaged 8% over ten years against an estimated 13% cost of capital, its market share has fallen every year for five years, and it has just announced a large debt-funded capacity expansion. What is the most likely conclusion?
options: A bargain: the low multiples provide a margin of safety
A value trap: returns below the cost of capital, falling share and an expansion that will destroy more value
Fairly valued, since 7 times earnings is close to the market average
Impossible to judge without a DCF
body.explanation: Persistent returns below the cost of capital justify a low multiple. Falling market share suggests structural, not cyclical, weakness. And a debt-funded expansion at those returns destroys further value, because each new rupee invested earns less than it costs.

body.title: The return identity
body.textWithBlank: Over the long run, total return is approximately earnings growth plus dividend yield plus the change in the ___.
body.explanation: Buying at a multiple that later contracts can turn good earnings growth into a poor return, and buying at a depressed multiple that expands can do the opposite.

body.title: Three traps in one stock
body.scenario: Nandini, an investor in Nagpur, is considering a listed textile exporter. It trades at 6 times trailing earnings, its lowest in a decade, and at 0.8 times book value. Last year was a record: margins reached 19% against a ten-year average of 10%, helped by a weak rupee and a competitor's factory fire. ROCE has averaged 9% over ten years against an estimated 13% cost of capital. The company has announced a ₹2,000 crore debt-funded expansion and has issued fresh equity twice in five years at prices below book value. A brokerage note argues for a target price based on the stock returning to its ten-year median P/E of 14.
body.prompt: Identify the traps in this investment case and set out how Nandini should value the company.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Peak margins. A 19% margin against a ten-year average of 10% reflects a weak rupee and a competitor's temporary shutdown, neither of which is permanent. The "6 times earnings" is calculated on peak profits, so the real multiple on normalised earnings is far higher.
2. Value trap characteristics. ROCE of 9% against a 13% cost of capital means the business destroys value on the capital it employs, which justifies a low multiple rather than signalling a bargain.
3. Value-destroying growth. A ₹2,000 crore debt-funded expansion at those returns makes matters worse, not better, and raises financial risk.
4. Dilution. Two equity issues below book value in five years have transferred value from existing shareholders. Any valuation must use fully diluted shares and assume further raises if cash flow does not cover the expansion.
5. Multiple mean reversion. The brokerage target assumes a return to a ten-year median P/E of 14, which was set when conditions were different. Applying a median multiple to peak earnings compounds two errors at once.

How to value it: normalise earnings to a 10% margin; check whether ROCE can rise above the cost of capital, and if not, treat growth as value-destroying; value on a mid-cycle EV/EBITDA and on P/B against normalised ROE, which for a company earning below its cost of capital justifies a multiple below 1; model dilution explicitly; and only then compare with the market price. The honest conclusion may be that 6 times peak earnings is expensive.

body.title: Ten questions before you act on any valuation
steps: Are this year's margins near the multi-year average, or near a peak or trough?
Is ROCE above the cost of capital, through a full cycle?
Does growth create value, or does it consume capital at low returns?
Do profits turn into cash over a ten-year period?
What does the current multiple imply about growth and returns, on a reverse DCF?
If I am relying on a historical multiple, has anything structural changed since then?
Have I used a fully diluted share count, and modelled future capital raises?
Did I set the discount rate before seeing the answer?
Have I double counted growth, cash or the tax shield anywhere?
Am I presenting a range and a bear case, rather than a single number?

points: Most valuation errors come from treating temporary conditions as permanent, or ignoring permanent problems.
Peak margins are the most expensive single mistake: normalising a margin from 18% to 11% cut value by nearly 40% in this lesson's example.
A cheap multiple is not a margin of safety when returns on capital sit below the cost of capital. Growth then makes the problem worse.
Total return is roughly growth plus yield plus the change in the multiple. A derating can cancel out strong earnings growth.
Value per share, not total value, is what you own. Model dilution from equity raises and ESOPs.
Set your discount rate before you see the answer, quote ranges rather than precise numbers, and check for double counting.
